reply.text: `==` tests whether two objects have equal values, calling the `__eq__` method, which can be customized by the class. `is` tests whether two names refer to the exact same object in memory, comparing identity (which `id()` exposes). Two equal values can be distinct objects, so `[1, 2] == [1, 2]` is `True` but `[1, 2] is [1, 2]` is `False`. `is` is the right tool for singletons like `None`, `True`, and `False` (write `x is None`, not `x == None`). Using `is` to compare numbers or strings is a bug: CPython caches some small ints and interned strings, so the result can look right in testing and break elsewhere.
